title: WHAT IF A STAR 350X THE SUN SWALLOWED YOU?

segments.line: You are a small star. And a giant star is swallowing you.
It weighs seven Suns, and it is three hundred fifty times wider.
This really happened. Astronomers watched it. The paper came out yesterday.
This really happened. Astronomers watched it. The paper came out yesterday.
It is two and a half million light-years away, in Andromeda.
So what if you rode the small star all the way down?
Here are the rules.
You are Little Bao. A star a bit smaller than our Sun.
Your friend is Big Bao. Big is the polite word.
You bring nothing. You are a star. You are the luggage.
You do not steer. Physics steers. Physics is not chatty.
The trip takes about seven years. Pack snacks.
First, meet the giant you are about to visit.
Big Bao is a red giant. A very, very old star, puffed up.
Big Bao is a red giant. A very, very old star, puffed up.
It weighs about seven Suns.
It is three hundred fifty times wider than the Sun.
Put it where our Sun is, and its surface would pass Mars.
Earth would be inside it. Along with everything you have ever met.
It is also eighteen thousand times brighter than the Sun.
Next to it, you are a pebble with a glow.
And you weigh about seventy percent of the Sun.
That is the first time anyone has ever measured you.
Scientists found your weight by doing their sums on the dust.
You two had been circling quietly for ages. Millennia, even.
Then your orbit dipped, just a little, and everything changed.
Then your orbit dipped, just a little, and everything changed.
Picture a spoon in thick soup.
Drag it through, and the soup pushes back.
That is you. The giant's outer layers are the soup.
In twenty eighteen your orbit starts brushing its outer atmosphere.
Drag. Slow, patient drag. Your orbit starts to shrink.
Drag. Slow, patient drag. Your orbit starts to shrink.
And the system begins to glow, very slowly, a little brighter.
Friction turns your orbital energy into light.
A star's version of rubbing your hands to warm them.
Nobody on Earth knows yet. But some telescopes are already looking.
In February twenty twenty-three, NASA's NEOWISE flags something odd.
In February twenty twenty-three, NASA's NEOWISE flags something odd.
Before twenty eighteen, the star was steady. Now it is not.
They keep watching. Which is the whole point of this story.
By September twenty twenty-four, a survey sees dust pouring off it.
You are leaking material, and it is getting crowded.
Now the lap count. A lap is one trip round the giant.
Lap one. You skim the atmosphere. Everything is fine.
Lap three. You are lower. The soup is thicker.
Lap five. The gas around you glows orange.
Each lap takes about a year. Each lap gets tighter.
Other star mergers took thousands of laps to happen.
Yours? About seven. Hold on to your halo.
The giant's gas drags you in like quicksand made of fire.
Lap six. You are almost at the centre.
In July twenty twenty-five, NASA's SPHEREx sees it fade in visible light.
In July twenty twenty-five, NASA's SPHEREx sees it fade in visible light.
And brighten in infrared. That swap is a loud alarm bell.
Dust is hiding the star's light. Something big is coming.
The astronomers do not know when. You know. It is lap seven.
The astronomers do not know when. You know. It is lap seven.
You touch the giant's surface, and the final plunge begins.
Down you go through the gas, faster and faster.
Above you, the whole star lights up.
Then, on the seventeenth of October twenty twenty-five, it erupts.
A flash that fills the sky of a galaxy.
In under a month, it brightens about a hundred times.
Someone spots it first. An amateur astronomer, with a flash of luck.
The team had been watching that very spot for years.
Nobody expected a bang in their lifetime. These stars stay calm for ages.
Nobody expected a bang in their lifetime. These stars stay calm for ages.
Luck. Patience. And a spreadsheet that never blinked.
Now, the race. Every telescope on call wants a look.
Now, the race. Every telescope on call wants a look.
The Zwicky Transient Facility confirms it on the seventeenth.
In November, NASA's Swift looks. So does Gemini North, in Hawaii.
In November, NASA's Swift looks. So does Gemini North, in Hawaii.
Every night, a new spectrum. Every spectrum, a new clue.
They all say the same thing: a smaller star fell into a giant.
But did you escape, or did you merge? Nobody knows yet.
Some pairs survive this dance. They end up in tight, shrunken orbits.
Some pairs survive this dance. They end up in tight, shrunken orbits.
So the telescopes need one more clue. A big one.
Enter the James Webb Space Telescope.
It wants to look at the dust the giant shed over centuries.
Dust holds the answer. How much dust, how much gas, how much star.
Dust holds the answer. How much dust, how much gas, how much star.
The date is the twenty-fourth of December. Christmas Eve.
That is forty-seven days after the peak.
The earliest anyone has ever followed up a merger like this.
What did Webb see? A tiny red-and-white dot, wrapped in dust.
The scientists ran their computer models over and over.
One model matched Webb's picture of the dust perfectly.
The model said you had enough energy left to flee.
But a deeper check said no.
You were dragged into the giant's core.
A Columbia scientist said: almost like a bomb inside a living star.
And you? You become part of the giant. One star, instead of two.
And you? You become part of the giant. One star, instead of two.
The blast threw off about a tenth of the giant's gas.
It flew away at roughly ten times escape speed.
Up and down it flew free. Old dust held back the middle.
The result looks a bit like a dusty hourglass in the sky.
You. A star. Gone, in seven years.
So why does this one matter?
This is called common envelope evolution.
It is how many tight pairs of stars get made.
Some of those pairs later become neutron stars. Or black holes.
Some send out ripples in space itself. Gravitational waves.
Until now, astronomers had to work backwards from old wreckage.
With you, they watched it live, before, during and after.
And it is not over. Bao's fate is still a mystery.
Dust hides the new star. It may take years, even decades, to settle.
Dust hides the new star. It may take years, even decades, to settle.
Soon there will be more. NASA's Roman telescope starts its surveys.
The lead author expects a large influx of similar discoveries.
Remember the first line? A small star, swallowed by a giant.
Now you know how a telescope, a spreadsheet and luck watched it happen.
Tomorrow: what if the Moon vanished for one night?
Would you ride the small star or the giant? Tell me below.
